title: How do you configure relationships and delete behavior in EF Core?
description: Navigations and foreign keys, one-to-many/many-to-many, cascade vs restrict, and delete-cycle traps.

data.text: **Question:** How do you configure relationships and delete behavior in EF Core?

EF Core maps relationships from **navigations + foreign keys** — conventions discover most of them, and the fluent API (`HasOne/HasMany/WithOne/WithMany`, `HasForeignKey`, `OnDelete`) makes them explicit. Delete behavior is a design decision: **Cascade** removes dependents automatically (convenient, but dangerous with cycles or bulk deletes), **Restrict** blocks the delete (safe default for optional relations), and you choose per relationship — not globally.

**Modeling:**
- Required FK: nullable navigation ≠ null → `IsRequired()`; optional: nullable FK column
- One-to-many: collection navigation on principal, reference on dependent; cascade is the default for **required** dependents
- One-to-one: `HasOne(a => a.Passport).WithOne(p => p.Owner).HasForeignKey<Passport>(p => p.OwnerId)`
- Many-to-many: skip navigations (`HasMany(p => p.Tags).WithMany(t => t.Posts)`) — EF creates the join table; add an entity for it when you need payload (rating, added-by, date)
- Alternate keys: `HasAlternateKey` for logical unique constraints referenced by other tables

**Delete behavior options:**
- **Cascade** — DB-level `ON DELETE CASCADE` (or client-side for cyclic models): deleting a Blog deletes its Posts. Convenient; risky: accidental mass deletes, and SQL Server forbids cascade paths that *cycle* (two cascading paths to one table → migration error)
- **Restrict** — FK violation if children exist; forces explicit cleanup. Preferred when children outlive parents (orders survive a deleted customer — actually then you'd **SetNull** or archive)
- **SetNull** — FK to null on delete (optional relations only)
- **ClientCascade** — EF performs the dependent deletes in the same transaction — needed when the database can't express the cascade (cycle), but you must **load the dependents** for it to work
- **NoAction** — the database does nothing; a dependent row then dangles/fails FK validation on save

**The traps:**
- Required dependents with `NoAction` → FK violations at SaveChanges, not at insert of the parent
- Cyclic relationships (A→B→A both required): SQL Server raises *multiple cascade paths* — model one side as Restrict/ClientCascade
- Bulk deletes bypass tracked cascades: `ExecuteDelete` won't cascade client-side for cycles — do it in SQL explicitly
- Deleting a principal with tracked dependents only works if they are loaded (client cascade) — otherwise FK errors

data.title: Explicit relationship and delete behavior

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Fluent API fluency: HasOne/WithMany/HasForeignKey/OnDelete
- Knowing each delete behavior and when to pick which
- Awareness of SQL Server's cascade-path cycle restriction and client cascade
- That many-to-many with payload means an explicit join entity

items: Accepting the cascade default everywhere — deleting a parent silently wipes dependent history
Required FK + NoAction: FK errors appear only at SaveChanges
Hitting 'multiple cascade paths' errors and not understanding they're a SQL Server rule
Assuming ExecuteDelete/SQL DELETE triggers client-side cascades for cyclic models
Leaving dependents unloaded while relying on ClientCascade
Modeling many-to-many payload (votes, timestamps) without an explicit join entity
Orders must survive customer deletion — how do you model that?
How do you handle two required entities referencing each other?
What's the difference between what EF does and what the database does on cascade delete?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Relationships = navigations + FK, made explicit with the fluent API
Cascade / Restrict / SetNull / ClientCascade / NoAction — choose per relation
Cyclic required relations break SQL Server cascades — split the behavior
Client cascades only delete what is loaded; bulk SQL bypasses them
data.takeaway: Deleting rows is a business rule: pick delete behavior deliberately so history, mass-deletes, and database limits all stay under control.
